It solves the problem of mapping continuous geometric primitives to a discrete pixel buffer by projecting vertices and interpolating face attributes, rather than simulating light transport [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that rasterization 'exploits the geometric properties of objects' (vertices and faces) to create an image, involving transforming vertices, projecting them to image coordinates, and interpolating depth on face primitives. It also explicitly contrasts this with ray casting, noting that rasterization 'does not try to emulate the image formation process of the real world' (which involves light transport) and is 'harder to capture certain effects using it (e.g., lighting effects, shadows, reflections)' compared to ray casting. Thus, the claim that it solves the mapping problem by projecting/interpolating rather than simulating light transport is fully supported by the text.
